extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing fiction writers (especially horror/fantasy) and readers interested in writing craft
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative guidance for writing short stories and novels in horror/fantasy (craft, process, career strategy). The page is an interview covering character work, plotting vs discovery, revision, genre, and practical career milestones.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-concept plus strong characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to come up with a concept that feels exciting and fresh, but couple it with characters the reader cares about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joe Hill: “It’s great to have a high concept, a sticky high concept... but I need characters to care about.” A high-concept premise is useful to hook readers/market the book, but it is not sufficient; characters must carry the long work. Examples: a worldwide pathogen that causes spontaneous combustion is an exciting idea, but you still need characters with interior life to sustain the novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters as mysteries / deep interiority
rubrics_metrics.description: View each character as a puzzle or mystery to be picked apart: know what excites them, what breaks their heart, their regrets and defenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joe Hill: “I actually view each character almost as a kind of mystery that I'm going to pick apart... what excites them, what breaks their heart, what has broken their heart?” Guidance includes building backstory, motivations, defeats, victories so that characters make convincing choices and remain interesting across months or years of writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let characters drive the plot; avoid forcing actions
rubrics_metrics.description: If characters are being forced to make choices they wouldn’t make, the story stalls; let characters choose and follow the consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hill: being stuck is often because “you’re trying to force your characters to do something that they don't want to do.” Antipattern: rigidly steering characters toward planned scenes. Positive pattern: accept when characters ‘turn left’ — this often leads to more authentic, more interesting scenes than your planned path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery writing (minimal outlining) over rigid outlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer discovery/‘pantsing’ where the author discovers the story through characters rather than strictly plotting every beat in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hill: “I think outlines are garbage... I don't ever outline.” Start with a concept and characters and allow the narrative to reveal itself. That said, you can keep a few set pieces or events you want to reach; outlines need not be mandatory, but heavy reliance on them can hamstring character-driven discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iteration, failure as training (lift to failure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat early/bad work as training; failed stories and novels are raw material and muscle-building for future, better work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hill: “All the bad stories were early drafts of good stuff... lift to failure... You built muscle.” Practical guidance: repurpose locations/objects/characters from unpublished or failed projects into new works; don’t regard early failure as wasted time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write what you actually love (permission to write)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give yourself permission to write the kinds of stories you enjoy reading rather than what you think you should write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hill’s pen name freed him to write horror: he stopped trying to write New Yorker-style fiction and returned to the horror/fantasy he loved. Anti-pattern: forcing yourself into genres or modes you don't read or enjoy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and protect your own voice; avoid imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate a personal voice; reading or admiring other writers is useful, but don't try to write exactly like them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hill: “my voice... it's just the way I write... I can't write like Keith.” Read to absorb techniques (see fair-play mysteries example) but keep your own sentence rhythm and sensibility; imitation often rings false on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence-level craft / polish
rubrics_metrics.description: Work on sentence-by-sentence quality—clarity, rhythm, word choice—even early in your career.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hill notes being ‘pretty polished’ on sentences by his early 20s. Even if larger-story skills lag, technical craft at the sentence level strengthens everything and is a defendable skill to build.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define success by craft milestones (finishing) not external metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure success by the act of making the art and finishing work rather than sales, reviews, or bestseller lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: “the only success... is making the art itself. It is finishing that story.” Practical advice: set achievable goals (finish a scene, finish a draft, place a story in a small anthology) and re-evaluate success expectations to avoid discouragement from external metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repurpose elements from earlier projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Reuse promising settings, characters, or objects from unpublished/failed projects in later works where they may fit better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hill reused the location 'The Briars' and a supernatural object ('the surrealist glass') from earlier failed novels in King Sorrow. Treat earlier drafts as a toolbox for future stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be free to blend genres; don’t be limited by labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't let rigid marketing/genre categories restrict creative choice—mix horror, fantasy, and other modes as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hill discusses how King Sorrow mixes horror and fantasy (dragon vs. horror tropes) and argues that genre labels are often marketing conveniences rather than firm artistic boundaries. Encouragement to combine 'chocolate and peanut butter' rather than force a single category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read targetedly to learn structures and techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Read widely within and beyond your preferred genre to absorb specific techniques and narrative forms (e.g., fair-play mysteries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hill cites Fangoria for horror-movie literacy and Anthony Horowitz/fair-play mysteries as models he absorbed. Read with attention to structure and mechanics you want to emulate, not just surface effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use other media/formats (e.g., comics) as experimental labs
rubrics_metrics.description: Try techniques and subgenres in other formats (graphic novels, short comics) before committing them to long-form novels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hill used comics to experiment with fair-play mysteries and other forms; some experiments may not land commercially but provide valuable practice and lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and observation to inhabit unfamiliar characters
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing characters with lives unlike your own, use research and observation to render them authentically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Hill read Rolling Stone and other sources to inhabit a heavy-metal musician character. Practical approaches: read trade magazines, interviews, watch documentaries, and observe real-world behavior to supply believable detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persist through rejections; aim for achievable milestones
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep writing despite rejections and set intermediate goals (e.g., place a story in an anthology) to build career momentum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hill recounts targeting a specific anthology as a marker of success early in his career. Advice: redefine success to maintain motivation, celebrate small wins, and keep producing work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice read-aloud performance and delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop oral delivery skills by reading aloud—practice improves public readings and helps shape sentence rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hill attributes early family read-alouds to his later comfort with public readings. Guidance: rehearse aloud, time passages, and use vocal practice to refine how prose sounds to an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the story contain its own solutions (look for baked-in answers)
rubrics_metrics.description: When blocked, look back—often the narrative already contains foreshadowing or the logical solution to your problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hill: “I'll often find that the solution is already baked into the story... the character is already foreshadowed.” Antipattern: inventing contrived fixes; instead search the existing material for authentic leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take creative risks and step outside your comfort zone
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasionally attempt projects that swing away from your established audience or style to grow as a writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hill tried a comic about a cop-turned-comic and a fair-play mystery that didn't fully land with his readership but taught him craft lessons. Encouragement: risk-taking can yield useful experience even if a project 'belly-flops.'
